title: If we look too hard for reality, we’ll fall into a black hole
subtitle: Quantum Gravity begins where measurement ends
author: Daniel Carney
introduction: Try to measure an object’s location too precisely, and you’ll collapse into a black hole. Physicist Daniel Carney highlights this overlooked consequence of quantum mechanics and general relativity, suggesting that it reveals many basic physical quantities to be fundamentally approximate. The path to a theory of quantum gravity, he argues, hinges on confronting the limits of measurement and observation—and perhaps leads to the realisation that ultimate reality lies forever beyond observation.
body:
Measurement in quantum mechanics and general relativity

Our understanding of the universe is limited by how precisely we can measure physical systems. Without the microscope, the cellular underpinnings of life could never have been learned; without the telescope, determining if the dots of light in the night sky are stars or some kind of celestial lightning bug would have been impossible. In practice, we make better measurements by developing new technologies and devices. But the same laws of physics govern both the observed systems and the devices used to observe them. An important, elementary question thus arises: are there fundamental physical limitations to what can be detected with a measurement apparatus, even in principle.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Dimensions of the unknown With Robert Lawrence Kuhn, Raphael Bousso, Dean Rickles, Karen Crowther

Addressing this question in full will require the union of our two most fundamental frameworks of nature: quantum mechanics and the general theory of relativity. Roughly speaking, general relativity—Einstein's theory of gravity—tells us where and when we can measure, and quantum mechanics tells us that the outcomes of measurements must follow certain probabilistic and often counter-intuitive rules. Gravitational event horizons, such as those experienced by an observer who remains outside of a black hole, delineate parts of spacetime which that observer can never access even in principle. Quantum mechanics teaches us that measurements always give at least slightly uncertain answers, and that the act of observation necessarily disturbs the state of the observed system.

Any measurement device has mass, and thus gravitates. It must also obey the laws of quantum mechanics. Do these facts imply anything about how well a measurement can be done? Thinking about situations in which both the gravity and quantum mechanics of the observational apparatus are important may sound esoteric. Gravity is most pronounced in large systems, like planets and galaxies. Quantum mechanics, on the other hand, reveals its mysteries most visibly in tiny, isolated objects like individual atoms. Yet today we have a variety of measurement devices, used in actual laboratories, where both quantum and gravitational effects are present.

We have predicted a limit to how well the position of an object can ever be measured: if we try to observe its location too precisely, the object will collapse into a black hole.

An important and famous example is the detection of small forces acting on objects, such as those exerted by gravitational waves, first detected by the LIGO collaboration in 2015. A passing gravitational wave causes all massive objects in its path to move slightly, and this is how the wave is detected. In LIGO, the moving masses are mirrors hung on wires. The motion generated by gravitational waves is measured by reflecting light off the mirrors and checking how long it takes to return. When a gravitational wave passes, the mirror moves by about 0.1 billion billionth (10^-19) of a meter, about 1000 times less distance than the width of an atom's nucleus. So it should not surprise you to learn that this measurement displays distinctly quantum mechanical effects. At the same time, the mirror itself is enormous for a quantum system: about 40 kilograms, the weight of a small person! Thus, this system of mirrors and lasers is observably quantum mechanical, but also big enough that its gravitational field can be easily measured.

Understanding the logical limits of such measurement systems is an under-explored direction in physics, which may have profound consequences for our understanding of the quantum mechanics of gravity itself. Today, we lack a detailed, self-consistent theory which can tell us how measurements involving very massive quantum systems would work in full generality, let alone any experiments probing this issue directly. Models of quantum gravity like string theory may be able to provide answers in specific contexts, but even there, we have only limited theoretical information. At present, we can only speculate qualitatively, piecing together bits of intuition from quantum and gravitational systems that we currently understand using separate theories.

The limits of measurement and the loss of reality

So what would this kind of intuition lead us to anticipate in a full theory of quantum gravity? Consider again the example we just gave, where we measure the position of a mirror by shining light on it. In quantum mechanics, the position of the mirror necessarily has some tiny uncertainty. What happens if we try to measure the position better, further decreasing this position uncertainty? Heisenberg's uncertainty principle implies that this would cause the uncertainty of the velocity of the mirror to increase in inverse proportion. And this is where gravity comes in: this would in turn imply that the mirror’s energy was becoming more and more uncertain, and eventually there would be a large probability that the measurement device itself would have so much energy that it would collapse to form a black hole!

The very notion of space might be, at best, an approximate concept.

The interpretation of this argument is somewhat subtle. A conservative way to phrase it is that we have predicted a limit to how well the position of an object can ever be measured: if we try to observe its location too precisely, the object will collapse into a black hole. This would already be a remarkable conclusion that goes beyond the basic tenets of quantum mechanics itself, which in principle allow for arbitrarily precise measurements. It is a prediction about what happens to measurements in a theory merging quantum mechanics with gravity.

However, depending on one's philosophical leanings, the implications of this may be much more radical. It is tempting to speculate that measurements are just lossy images of some underlying reality. But a common view among physicists, going back to Schrodinger and exemplified by John Bell, is that “reality” is nothing more than the sum total of what can be measured. And from this viewpoint, what we have found is an argument that the very notion of space might be, at best, an approximate concept. If space cannot be measured to arbitrary accuracy without forming a black hole, then in a minimal interpretation of what it means for something to exist, space simply does not exist at arbitrarily small length scales.

Measurement of any quantity to arbitrary precision would eventually require so much energy that the apparatus would collapse to form a black hole. This is a wild departure from traditional notions of physics.

While we have been discussing the measurement of positions of objects, the basic idea is much more general. Measurement of any quantity to arbitrary precision would eventually require so much energy that the apparatus would collapse to form a black hole. This is a wild departure from traditional notions of physics. We have always operated under the assumption that, in principle, observable quantities can be specified to arbitrary precision. The value of the electric field at a point can be written E=2.59185... V/m, and the digits can go on forever. But the arguments above lead to a wild conclusion: eventually, the dots stop. Reality is, in some sense, finite. And if this is really the case, the observable quantities we have been using to formulate physics for the past four centuries must all end up being approximate in a fundamental sense.

These ideas about measurement are intimately tied to other arguments stemming from the physics of black holes. As early as the 1960s, Bekenstein and Hawking gave theoretical evidence that implies that the amount of information that can be stored behind the event horizon of a black hole is finite. Our only detailed model of quantum gravity, string theory, confirms this idea in great detail in certain examples. And since the 1997 discovery that the universe is undergoing accelerated expansion, we know that we also live inside an event horizon, because distant light rays cannot catch up to the speed of expansion, and thus cannot reach us. This implies that the amount of information we can ever access in the observable universe should likewise be finite. This all seems to suggest that our traditional notion of infinitely precise observable quantities in physics is fundamentally wrong (although it is accurate to a very high degree, so that current experiments are not yet sensitive to this kind of bound on information).

The path forward

An ambitious direction would be to experimentally search for effects of these fundamental limitations on measurement. There are a handful of highly speculative ideas in this direction. For example, Hogan, and more recently Verlinde and Zurek, have suggested that limits on the information content within the finite region of spacetime accessible to a real experiment could lead to relatively large effects, such as fluctuations in distances measured by a device like LIGO. An experiment in the 2010s at Fermilab called the Holometer failed to find any evidence of this, while a newer, more sensitive version of this experiment, GQuEST, is currently under construction at the California Institute of Technology. But interpreting the results of these measurements is murky. The predicted fluctuations are not based on any detailed theory of quantum gravity. Much like the arguments presented above, the idea comes from piecing together implications of quantum and gravitational theory in a shoot-from-the-hip fashion, rather than from a precise and general theory.

All of the above points to an urgent need to substantially develop our theory of measurement in quantum, gravitating systems. Very recently, there has been a great deal of activity in this direction, particularly in identifying effects of physical gravitating observers within quantum gravity. But the results are primitive, and far from being able to produce any precise experimental predictions. Much more work is needed to model how a physical, quantum-mechanical detector gravitates. The kinds of questions that need answers are deceptively simple: for example, is it really true that, within the context of a detailed model like string theory, trying to measure the position of a LIGO mirror more and more accurately would cause the device to collapse into a black hole? Or could some more exotic phenomenon occur? These types of questions should have concrete answers within the theory itself. And then, with this kind of theoretical toolbox in hand, we can start searching for motivated examples to pursue with experiments in the real world.
